result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.small_world_sigma()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the small-world coefficient sigma. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L28192-L28263){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.small_world_sigma( niter=100, nrand=10, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Small-world coefficient sigma](/assets/graphs/small-world-sigma.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="An eight-node ring with four chords that close four triangles. Its transitivity C is 0.43, against 0.354 averaged over 10 degree-preserving random references, while its average path length L, 1.643, is close to the references' 1.707. The card divides the two ratios, (0.43 / 0.354) / (1.643 / 1.707), for sigma = 1.260: above 1, so the graph counts as small-world." width="100%"} A small-world network combines the high clustering of a lattice with the short paths of a random graph. Humphries and Gurney (2008) measure this as $$\sigma = \frac{C / C_r}{L / L_r},$$ where $C$ is the transitivity and $L$ the average shortest path length, and $C_r$, $L_r$ are their averages over `nrand` random reference graphs with the same degrees (see `random_reference()`). A network is commonly called small-world when $\sigma > 1$: clustered well beyond chance while keeping near-random path lengths. Typical uses are brain, social and infrastructure networks. The graph must be undirected and connected, and is treated as simple. The result is random; use `seed=` for reproducible values. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [niter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Rewiring rounds for each random reference (default 100, as in NetworkX). [nrand]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[10]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of random references to average (default 10). [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The coefficient sigma. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or disconnected, or has fewer than four nodes or two edges. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Follows NetworkX's `sigma`, with the rewiring and the metrics computed in Rust, which makes it practical on graphs of a few thousand nodes (each reference needs all-pairs breadth-first searches for $L_r$). Because the references are random, values from EdgeCase and NetworkX agree only up to sampling noise. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A Watts-Strogatz graph with a little rewiring is strongly small-world: ::: {#3d859ea6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_smallworld_graph(n=100, k=6, p=0.1, seed=1) round(g.small_world_sigma(niter=10, nrand=5, seed=2), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 7.58 ``` ::: :::
